excerpt: A denied injury claim is not the end. How to read the denial letter, what to gather, how to press for reconsideration, and when a regulatory complaint or a lawsuit is the next step.
keyTakeaways: A denied claim is not the end. Steps include reviewing the denial letter, gathering evidence, asking for reconsideration in writing, complaining to the state insurance regulator, and filing suit before the deadline. Bad-faith remedies run against your own insurer, not the other driver's: Georgia's O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6 gives a policyholder up to 50% of the loss or $5,000, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees after a 60-day demand; South Carolina awards attorney's fees after a 90-day demand (S.C. Code § 38-59-40) and recognizes a bad-faith tort (Nichols v. State Farm). Georgia's 2-year and South Carolina's 3-year filing deadlines are not extended by a denial.

faqs.question: Why was my claim denied?
faqs.answer: Common reasons include disputed liability, pre-existing conditions, treatment gaps, missed deadlines, policy exclusions, and insufficient evidence. The denial letter should state the reason.

faqs.question: Can I appeal a denied claim?
faqs.answer: You can ask the insurer to reconsider — there is no formal appeal of a liability insurer's denial in Georgia or South Carolina, but a written request with new evidence that answers each stated reason can change the outcome. If it does not, you can complain to the state insurance regulator (the Office of the Commissioner of Insurance and Safety Fire in Georgia; the Department of Insurance in South Carolina) and, before the deadline runs, file suit against the at-fault party.

faqs.question: What is bad faith denial in Georgia?
faqs.answer: Georgia's bad-faith statute protects policyholders against their own insurer. Under O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6, if your insurer refuses in bad faith to pay a covered claim within 60 days of your written demand, it owes the claim plus a penalty of up to 50% of the loss or $5,000, whichever is greater, and your attorney's fees (on uninsured-motorist claims, up to 25% or $25,000 under § 33-7-11(j)). It does not let you sue the other driver's insurer for denying your claim.

faqs.question: What is bad faith denial in South Carolina?
faqs.answer: South Carolina's improper-claim-practices statute, S.C. Code § 38-59-20, is enforced by the Department of Insurance and gives no private claim. A policyholder whose own insurer refuses to pay for 90 days after a demand, without reasonable cause or in bad faith, recovers attorney's fees under § 38-59-40, and under Nichols v. State Farm can sue for the bad-faith denial itself — consequential damages and, for willful or reckless conduct, punitive damages capped by § 15-32-530. South Carolina does not allow a bad-faith suit against the other driver's insurer.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file a lawsuit?
faqs.answer: Georgia: 2 years from date of injury (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). South Carolina: 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). The denial does not restart or extend these deadlines.

faqs.question: Should I hire a lawyer after a denial?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. A denied claim is not the end. An attorney can identify the issue, gather evidence, press the insurer to reconsider, bring a bad-faith claim against your own insurer where the facts support one, and take the case against the at-fault party to trial. We handle denied claims on contingency — you pay nothing unless we recover.
